blocks.content: A registry is a server that stores Docker images and lets you push them up or pull them down by name and tag. It is the piece of infrastructure that turns "an image on my machine" into "an image any machine can fetch."

At its core, a registry is a storage and distribution system for images. docker push uploads an image to a registry, docker pull downloads one from it. Without a registry, sharing an image with a teammate or a production server would mean manually copying image files around, which does not scale past a single laptop.

blocks.alt: Push uploads, pull downloads, the registry sits in between

blocks.content: Docker Hub is the best known public registry, free to use for public images. For proprietary application code, teams almost always use a private registry instead, options include cloud-native ones like Amazon ECR or Google Artifact Registry, or a self-hosted registry running inside your own infrastructure.

blocks.alt: Public registries for open images, private ones for everything else

blocks.content: Inside a registry, images are organized by repository (the name, like myapp) and tag (the version, like 1.0 or latest). The same repository can hold many tagged versions, letting you pull an exact version instead of whatever happens to be newest.

blocks.alt: One repository, many tagged versions inside it

blocks.content:
docker pull myapp:1.0        # a specific, known version
docker pull myapp:latest     # whatever was most recently tagged "latest"
docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

code.content:
docker pull myapp:1.0        # a specific, known version
docker pull myapp:latest     # whatever was most recently tagged "latest"
docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

codes.bash:
docker pull myapp:1.0        # a specific, known version
docker pull myapp:latest     # whatever was most recently tagged "latest"
docker tag myapp:1.0 myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0
docker push myregistry.com/team/myapp:1.0

blocks.content: Private registries require authentication before you can push or pull. docker login sends your credentials to the registry, which issues back a token the client then uses for subsequent requests, so you are not re-entering a password on every single push.

blocks.alt: Login once, the client reuses the token afterward

blocks.content: 5. The Registry in a Real Deployment Pipeline
blocks.text: 5. The Registry in a Real Deployment Pipeline

blocks.content: In a typical CI/CD setup, a pipeline builds an image from your code, pushes it to a private registry, and then the production environment pulls that exact same image from the registry to run it. The registry is the handoff point between "built by CI" and "running in production."

blocks.alt: The registry is the handoff between CI and production

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A registry is what turns a locally built image into something any authorized machine can fetch by name and tag.
Production deployments almost always go through a private registry, the registry is the handoff point between "CI built this" and "production is running this."
